results.title: "Is EU4 Only About Map Painting?": Settler Colonial Ideology in Europa Universalis IV
results.preview:
It aims to show that this account is one which is predicated off settler colonial attitudes. To do so, this project will interrogate the game in terms of its settler colonial gameplay systems and the ways in which players interact with these systems. The two main chapters will more deeply explore these themes, exploring both how the game is a contemporary wargame, how settler colonial modes represent themselves in the underlying code, and the manners in which players navigate these modes through writing "After Action Reports" and modding. The thesis concludes by thinking about how incorporating perspectives from indigenous creators and settler colonial theorists might help move the game from being just about conquering a map and toward a more cohesive, authentic account of the game's historical moment.

- Description

Assistant Professor

Department of Informatics

University of California, Irvine

Aaron Trammell is an assistant professor of Informatics at UC Irvine. He graduated from the Rutgers University School of Communication and Information in 2015 and spent a year at the Annenberg School of Communication at USC as a postdoctoral researcher. Aaron's research is focused on revealing historical connections between games, play, and the United States military-industrial complex. He is interested in how political and social ideology is integrated in the practice of game design and how these perspectives are negotiated within the imaginations of players. He is the Editor-in-Chief of the journal Analog Game Studies and the Multimedia Editor of Sounding Out!

The thesis concludes by thinking about how incorporating perspectives from indigenous creators and settler colonial theorists might help move the game from being just about conquering a map and toward a more cohesive, authentic account of the game's historical moment.

windows.title: Gaming History Quiz: What was the first expansion pack/free DLC/paid DLC ever released?
windows.text:
title: Gaming History Quiz: What was the first expansion pack/free DLC/paid DLC ever released?
author: Infinitron
date: 2013-01-11
---
- Joined

- Jan 28, 2011

- Messages

- 102,010

Definitions:

We'll define "expansion pack" as something that was sold in boxes, in a store.

We'll define "DLC" as something that was only available via download. DLC that was at first only available via download, but was released in a box later on, still counts as DLC.

Questions:

1) What was the first expansion pack that was actually a separate new campaign? Ie, a "sequel expansion", not something that altered any of the original game's content.

2) What was the first expansion pack that added content to the original game? This can be anything from horse armor to new quests to new classes and mechanics.

3) What was the first free DLC that was a separate new campaign?

4) What was the first free DLC that added content to the the original game?

5) What was the first paid DLC that was a separate new campaign?

6) What was the first paid DLC that added content to the original game?

Possible issues:

Sometimes the separation between "separate adventure" and "added content" can get murky. For example, in Icewind Dale, you can access the Heart of Winter expansion pack in Kuldahar, so arguably it "adds content" to the original game. But it's also a separate adventure accessible from the main menu. Then there's Throne of Bhaal which has both a separate adventure (Throne of Bhaal proper) and added content (Watcher's Keep). I think we can handle these on a case-by-case, common sense basis.

windows.title: Screen Rant
windows.text:
That sort of continuity helped to make the DLC the perfect thing to tide gamers over until the sequel could be developed.

Civilization IV (2005) - Beyond The Sword

Generally considered one of the best 4X games of all time, Civilization IV still had room for additional improvement when its second expansion, Beyond the Sword, was released. User MarioFanaticXV sang the expansion's praise, saying, "Beyond the Sword added more of everything- it expanded on what was already arguably the best Civ game".

Adding something new to almost every aspect of the game, Beyond the Sword not only improved the gameplay but made it more challenging as well. New scenarios and abilities allowed for additional strategies for victory, and a host of randomized events meant that seasoned players could still be caught off guard.

Borderlands 2 (2012) - Tiny Tina's Assault On Dragon Keep

Borderlands 2 was a hit on its own, but it presented fans with a host of DLC to keep them hunting vaults for years after its initial release. Praising one expansion in particular, user Mophmeister said Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep wrote, "Great setting, tons of content. Real shame the other BL2 DLC wasn't this good."

Drawing inspiration from TTRPGs, the expansion packed an emotional wallop and fleshed out the death of Roland. Usually ranked among the best DLC in the entire Borderlands series, Tiny Tina was spun off into her own title, and the Assault on Dragon Keep DLC has since been made available as a stand-alone game.

Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 (2000) - Yuri's Revenge

The early years of the 2000s were the dawn of the expansion pack and DLC, and games like Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 set the bar quite high.

DLC, or downloadable content, refers to additional content gamers download for video games after their initial release. This content may include new levels, characters, weapons, or skins.

DLC (Downloadable Content) is when you PAY to gain access to additional maps, skins, or modes.

Increased carrying capacity for players in raid when purchased: DLC

Special radio item with stats and effects when purchased: DLC

Special game mode when purchased: 110% DLC

Increased Fence rep when paid for: DLC

Special items: DLC

Increased mail claim time: DLC

Aaron Trammell is an assistant professor of Informatics at UC Irvine. He graduated from the Rutgers University School of Communication and Information in 2015 and spent a year at the Annenberg School of Communication at USC as a postdoctoral researcher. Aaron's research is focused on revealing historical connections between games, play, and the United States military-industrial complex. He is interested in how political and social ideology is integrated in the practice of game design and how these perspectives are negotiated within the imaginations of players. He is the Editor-in-Chief of the journal Analog Game Studies and the Multimedia Editor of Sounding Out!
